title: Quantum Oncology
subtitle: Cancer biology, clinical evidence and computation for quantum people — and a research method sound enough to publish on.
summary: You already know qubits, VQE and QAOA. This course supplies the other half: how cancer works, how it is diagnosed, treated and trialled, what classical computation already does in oncology, and exactly where quantum methods might — and might not — add something. Every claim is sourced and dated in the ledger. Five labs run real models in your browser, each unit ends with homework, and the capstone is a research proposal you can turn into a paper.
outcomes: Explain cancer at the level a referee in oncology expects: genes, hallmarks, clonal evolution, staging, treatment and resistance.
Read and run the statistics oncology lives on — Kaplan–Meier, log-rank, hazard ratios, trial power — on a real 1963 trial.
Map quantum algorithms (phase estimation, VQE, QAOA and annealing, quantum kernels, Born machines) onto concrete oncology problems, with resource estimates.
Benchmark honestly: strong classical baselines, ablations, leakage-free validation, simulability checks and the right reporting guideline.
Audit quantum-oncology claims, from preprints to press releases, separating demonstrations, estimates and contested results.
Write a publishable research proposal at the quantum–oncology interface.
prerequisites: Quantum computing to graduate level: circuits, VQE, QAOA, error correction
No biology or medicine needed — it is all taught here

outputs.title: Lab notebook
outputs.description: Your saved results from the five labs — tumour growth, survival, leakage, VQE and the gene panel — each with your interpretation and the limits of the model.

outputs.title: Homework problem sets
outputs.description: Written homework for every unit: derivations, calculations, short essays and paper-reading exercises, building the vocabulary and judgement a co-author needs.

outputs.title: Referee report
outputs.description: A structured peer review of the quantum-assisted KRAS inhibitor paper (Nature Biotechnology, 2025): claims, evidence, controls, and what you would ask the authors.

outputs.title: Headline audit
outputs.description: An audit of one real quantum-oncology announcement: the claim, the comparator, the scale, the simulability, the evidence level and your verdict.

outputs.title: Research proposal
outputs.description: Your publication blueprint: question, background, quantum method, classical baselines, data, benchmark protocol, ethics, reporting standard, abstract and target venue — with your lab results as pilot evidence.

units.title: Quantum oncology: the map
units.summary: What the phrase covers — computing, sensing, quantum biology and outright pseudoscience — and the scale of the disease.

units.title: Cancer biology for physicists
units.summary: The cell as an information system, the hallmarks of cancer, and cancer as an evolutionary process written in mutations.

units.title: From tumour to patient
units.summary: Growth laws and treatment kinetics, then diagnosis, staging and the four pillars of treatment — and why tumours come back.

units.title: Clinical evidence
units.summary: How drugs are tested, why most fail, and survival analysis computed by hand on a real trial.

units.title: Computational oncology today
units.summary: The classical baseline any quantum method must beat: cancer data resources, machine learning and its traps, and computational drug discovery.

units.title: Quantum methods for oncology
units.summary: Quantum chemistry for cancer drugs and its resource bill, VQE on a real Hamiltonian, and quantum machine learning on omics — with the fine print.

units.title: Optimisation and generative design
units.summary: Biomarker panels, radiotherapy plans and docking as QUBOs; then a full case study of a quantum-assisted KRAS inhibitor campaign.

units.title: The field in 2026
units.summary: Quantum sensing and quantum biology, who is doing what (checked 11 October 2026), and how to read an announcement.

units.title: From question to publication
